audits.title: Antibiotic timing in neonates with suspected hospital-acquired infections.
audits.standard: Antibiotics started within 2 hours of suspected hospital-acquired infection
audits.setting: Neonatal intensive care nurseries (level II or III), Medical University of South Carolina
audits.intervention: Series of QI cycles: education, standardised evaluation process and an online computerised physician order entry system streamlining nursery and pharmacy workflow

cycle2.result: Median antibiotic delivery time 75 minutes, with reduced variation (P < .001).

audits.other_findings: Computerised order entry significantly improved writing of STAT orders (P < .0001).
audits.citation: Bissinger RL, Mueller M, Cox TH, Cahill J, Garner SS, Irving M, et al.. Antibiotic timing in neonates with suspected hospital-acquired infections. Adv Neonatal Care. 2013;13(1):22-8; quiz 29-30. doi:10.1097/anc.0b013e3182862c99. PMID: 23360855.

audits.title: A multifaceted intervention  to improve sepsis management  in general hospital wards with  evaluation using segmented  regression of interrupted time series.
audits.standard: Antibiotics within 4 hours of sepsis onset; also within 8 hours, medical review within 30 min, blood cultures before antibiotics, lactate measured
audits.setting: 22 medical, surgical and orthopaedic wards, Ninewells Hospital, Dundee

cycle1.result: Antibiotic administration frequently delayed (figures not given in abstract).

audits.intervention: Printed and electronic guidance, educational team meetings with baseline data, audit and monthly performance feedback.

cycle2.result: All outcome measures improved but differences were small and interrupted time series analysis did not attribute change to the intervention.

audits.other_findings: Authors suggest senior clinician involvement in feedback and iterative refinement might have helped.
audits.citation: Marwick CA, Guthrie B, Pringle JE, Evans JM, Nathwani D, Donnan PT, et al.. A multifaceted intervention  to improve sepsis management  in general hospital wards with  evaluation using segmented  regression of interrupted time series. BMJ Qual Saf. 2014;23(12):e2. doi:10.1136/bmjqs-2013-002176. PMID: 24259716.

audits.title: Electronic prescribing: Reducing delay to first dose of antibiotics for patients in intensive care.
audits.setting: Adult intensive care unit, Oxford University Hospitals NHS Trust

cycle1.result: Delays in antibiotic administration quantified (numbers not stated)

audits.intervention: Electronic prescribing system modified to remove default dose times so doses scheduled within an hour of prescription, plus enhanced training for clinicians and nurses

cycle2.result: Significant reduction in delays (p=0.002, Mann-Whitney U test)

audits.citation: Matthews PC, Wangrangsimakul T, Borthwick M, Williams C, Byren I, Wilkinson D. Electronic prescribing: Reducing delay to first dose of antibiotics for patients in intensive care. BMJ Qual Improv Rep. 2014;2(2):u202241.w1120. doi:10.1136/bmjquality.u202241.w1120. PMID: 26734229.

audits.title: Beating the clock: Reduced time to first antibiotic dose administration following an audit and feedback intervention.
audits.standard: First antibiotic dose within 3 hours of ordering
audits.setting: Surgical and medical wards, Soroka University Medical Center

cycle1.result: Longest delays on morning shift: 161 minutes (surgical) and 100 minutes (medical)

audits.intervention: Automated weekly audit and feedback email to nurse and physician leaders with percentage receiving first dose within 3 hours

cycle2.result: Morning shift time to first dose reduced by 87 minutes (55%) in surgical and 37 minutes (37%) in medical wards

audits.citation: Schlaeffer-Yosef T, Shafat T, Dreiher J, Cohen L, Codish S, Hadad H, et al.. Beating the clock: Reduced time to first antibiotic dose administration following an audit and feedback intervention. Int J Antimicrob Agents. 2023;62(1):106832. doi:10.1016/j.ijantimicag.2023.106832. PMID: 37121441.

audits.title: Faster administration of antimicrobials in sepsis team quality improvement initiative in the intensive care unit: a retrospective audit (FAAST-R).
audits.standard: Guideline first-dose antimicrobial timeframes: ≤60 min for sepsis or septic shock, ≤180 min without sepsis
audits.setting: Three adult ICUs, McGill University Health Centre

cycle1.result: Timely antimicrobials in 54% of sepsis or septic shock patients and 78% of patients without sepsis.

audits.other_findings: Longer time from pharmacist validation to administration and ongoing CRRT reduced odds of timely administration.
audits.citation: Duceppe MA, Baptista da Silva K, Wang H, Delucilla L, Rainone A, Couture I, et al.. Faster administration of antimicrobials in sepsis team quality improvement initiative in the intensive care unit: a retrospective audit (FAAST-R). Int J Pharm Pract. 2026. doi:10.1093/ijpp/riag096. PMID: 42476532.
